query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical behavior of pristine, solidified Co‐free equiatomic FeNiCrMn is controlled primarily by a thermally activated dislocation slip mechanism that is modulated by intrinsic lattice distortions and any short-range ordering. Temperature and strain rate variations alter the activation energy for dislocation motion, which in turn governs yield strength and work-hardening behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Pristine, fully solidified equiatomic Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with minimal extrinsic defects
generation.intervention: Systematically vary strain rate and temperature during tensile and/or compression tests while maintaining the alloy’s pristine state
generation.conditions: Tests conducted across a broad temperature range (from room temperature to ~1073 K) and over a wide range of strain rates from quasi-static to high dynamic rates, using specimens with controlled geometry and minimized defect populations
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsic dislocation structures, including dislocation density, configurations, and interactions as revealed by high-resolution TEM before and after deformation
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, increased lattice friction and drag retard dislocation motion, resulting in higher yield strength and enhanced work-hardening. At elevated temperatures, thermally activated processes lower the barriers to dislocation motion. This modulation is governed intrinsically by the lattice distortions and any short-range ordering present in the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength and strain-hardening rate will increase with increasing strain rate and decreasing temperature. Post-deformation TEM analyses should reveal higher dislocation densities and less mobile dislocation structures under high strain rate/low temperature conditions, consistent with an Arrhenius-type thermally activated dislocation mechanism.
generation.baseline: Pristine Co‐free FeNiCrMn tested under moderate temperature and strain-rate conditions where the standard strength–ductility balance is observed
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to fully solidified, undamaged equiatomic Co‐free FeNiCrMn. Any introduction of extrinsic defects or compositional modifications that significantly alter the intrinsic lattice distortion or short-range ordering may lead to deviations from the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in precisely quantifying the activation energies and in extending the observed behavior to extreme temperature/strain-rate regimes beyond those tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of pristine, fully solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn specimens with minimized extrinsic defects. Perform tensile and compression tests over a controlled range of temperatures (e.g., from room temperature to ~1073 K) and strain rates (from quasi-static to high dynamic rates). Conduct pre- and post-deformation high-resolution TEM analyses to quantify dislocation density and configurations.
measurements: Yield strength and work-hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Dislocation density and arrangement via TEM
Strain rate sensitivity and activation energy parameters derived from the deformation data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If temperature and strain rate variations do not yield a systematic, Arrhenius-type correlation between mechanical responses (yield strength and work-hardening) and changes in dislocation structure (i.e., if dislocation density/configuration remains invariant despite significant mechanical property changes), then the hypothesis that a thermally activated dislocation slip mechanism governs the dynamic behavior of Co‐free FeNiCrMn is falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies on high‐ and medium‐entropy alloys first demonstrated that complex phase equilibria (such as TRIP effects or precipitate strengthening) could be engineered via processing (e.g., friction stir processing or annealing) to impart both high strength and ductility. Later, researchers started to focus on dynamic behavior – testing at different strain rates and temperatures – and used in‐situ and atomistic simulation methods to reveal that dislocation‐based mechanisms (including slip, stacking fault generation, and even elastic instabilities) underlie the material response. However, these investigations were conducted in alloys with additional elements or processing‐induced defect states that obscure the intrinsic dynamic mechanism of a Co‐free system.
decision.unsolved: For equiatomic, solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the intrinsic mechanism governing the dynamic response across temperature and strain-rate regimes remains unresolved. In particular, it is unclear whether the response is controlled by a thermally activated dislocation mobility mechanism (modulated by inherent lattice distortion and short-range ordering) or by an alternative intrinsic instability, when extrinsic defects and compositional modifications are minimized.
decision.lever: Systematically vary strain rate and temperature on pristine, fully solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn specimens while controlling for extrinsic defect density, complemented by post‐deformation high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM for dislocation density and configurations) to correlate dynamic stress–strain responses with underlying dislocation mechanisms.
decision.why: This approach directly isolates the intrinsic behavior of the pristine FeNiCrMn alloy – keeping the Co-free and strength–ductility balance constraints intact – and builds on the prior trend of dynamic testing in related HEAs. By eliminating additional compositional or defect state complications present in earlier studies, it will allow researchers to test whether a thermally activated, dislocation-governed mechanism underlies the observed changes in dynamic behavior. A failure to correlate microstructural evolution with predicted strain-rate dependent activation parameters would falsify the hypothesis.
